trace.claim: The paper asks whether propagating stigmatizing labels like 'convicted criminal' on Trump in Democratic Party advertisements produces spillover effects that worsen Democrats' perceptions of individuals with criminal records more broadly, and whether perceived representation is affected.
The paper also asks whether providing a counter-narrative featuring a formerly system-involved representative can counteract the negative impacts of the stigmatizing advertisement.

Exposure to the Trump advertisement with the 'convicted criminal' label significantly worsened Democrats' perceptions of individuals with criminal records, while simultaneously improving perceived feelings of representation by elected officials.

A counter-narrative using perspective-getting with a formerly system-involved state representative substantially mitigated the negative effects of the advertisement on perceptions of individuals with criminal records.

The study employed a survey experiment with three randomly assigned treatment groups (Control, Trump Ad Alone, Counter-Narrative First) testing exposure to a real Democratic Party advertisement labeling Trump as a 'convicted criminal' and a perspective-getting counter-narrative about a formerly incarcerated state representative.
Data were collected via the Prolific online platform in July 2025 from 2,439 self-identified Democratic Party members residing in the United States who spoke fluent English.

Outcomes were measured using standardized indices and individual Likert-scale items covering perceptions of individuals with criminal records, value and quality of representation, complexity of representation, public-serving motives of elected officials, and advertisement support.

Exposure to the Trump advertisement alone significantly decreased positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records among Democrats by approximately 0.83 standard deviation units relative to the control group.

Presenting a perspective-getting counter-narrative before the advertisement increased positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records by more than 0.8 standard deviation units relative to the advertisement alone, essentially negating the advertisement's negative effect.

The Trump advertisement significantly increased Democrats' feelings of being well represented by elected officials and their perception that officials are motivated by public service rather than self-interest, suggesting a comparative benchmarking effect.
The counter-narrative significantly decreased Democrats' support for the use of the stigmatizing advertisement relative to those who saw the advertisement alone.

System-impacted individuals (those personally or through a loved one involved in the criminal justice system) reported significantly more positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records across all items and treatment arms, and showed greater sensitivity to the stigmatizing advertisement.

The study lacked a full factorial design, meaning the counter-narrative's independent effect (separate from the advertisement) cannot be isolated because the counter-narrative was always paired with the ad in that treatment arm.

Because the advertisement image (Trump's mugshot with the label) was held constant across all treatment arms, the study cannot disentangle the effect of the image from the effect of the stigmatizing terminology.
The study was conducted after the election outcome was known and not during an active campaign period, limiting external validity for understanding effects during live electoral competition.

The single time-point design leaves open questions about the durability of effects, how results vary with repeated exposure, and whether self-reported perceptions translate to actual behavioral changes.
The use of an online survey panel raises concerns about the potential influence of generative AI on responses, though the author notes Prolific has comparatively low AI infiltration rates.

The authors extend social categorization theory to a new domain—political messaging—arguing that the salient application of a stigmatizing label to a high-profile exemplar (Trump) produces spillover perceptions that worsen views of the broader category (individuals with criminal records).

The authors also invoke Prospect Theory to explain why the advertisement improved perceived representation, suggesting Trump serves as a low reference point against which other elected officials appear comparatively better.

The paper builds on the claim from the perspective-getting literature (attributed to Todd & Galinsky 2014 and Harney 2023) that being provided with another person's perspective significantly increases empathy for out-group members, including incarcerated individuals, and extends this finding to the context of mitigating stigma from political messaging about criminal records.

The paper draws on the meta-analytic finding attributed to Lau, Sigelman, and Rovner (2007) that negative campaign advertisements do not empirically support election success, using it to argue that the Democratic Party's stigmatizing strategy was counterproductive.
